results.title: Handling Missing Data in a Dataset: Imputation Methods Explained | by Abinaya Subramaniam | Learning Data | Medium
results.content: # Handling Missing Data in a Dataset: Imputation Methods Explained. Learn how to handle missing data in machine learning with effective strategies, including detection, understanding missingness types, and various imputation techniques. In this blog, we will explore the different types of missing data, their impact on machine learning models and various imputation methods. Data is considered MCAR if the missing values have no relationship with any other variables in the dataset. Data is MNAR if the missing values are dependent on unobserved information, making it the hardest type to handle. If missing values appear randomly across all rows and columns, the data is likely MCAR. However, if certain features show missing values in specific patterns, the data is more likely MAR or MNAR. There are several ways to handle missing data, ranging from simple deletion methods to advanced imputation techniques. KNN imputation replaces missing values based on the k most similar data points. Multiple Imputation generates multiple possible values for missing data and aggregates them for better accuracy.

results.title: How to decide whether missing values are MAR, MCAR, or MNAR (r,imputation, statistics) - Quora
results.content: * MAR: Missingness can depend on observed variables but not on the missing values themselves after conditioning on observed data. * MNAR: Missingness depends on the (unobserved) missing values themselves, even after conditioning on observed data. If you can make it plausible your data is mcar (non-significant little test) or mar, you can use multiple imputation to impute missing data. There are two rules that usually are followed: 1 never impute data for a response variable (y) as it will falselly increase your model fit; 2 if your missing data corresponds to a considerable ammount of data do not do it… You can limit ypir self to a given range (missing data up to 10-20% of your data), or better, in the end compare the results with and without imputed values, and with and without the corredponding variables to see if it's worth imputing the values and measure the bias created by imputation.

results.title: A hot deck imputation procedure for multiply imputing nonignorable missing data: The proxy pattern-mixture hot deck - ScienceDirect
results.content: # A hot deck imputation procedure for multiply imputing nonignorable missing data: The proxy pattern-mixture hot deck. Hot deck imputation is a common method for handling item nonresponse in surveys, but most implementations assume data are missing at random (MAR). A new hot deck method for imputation of a continuous partially missing outcome variable that harnesses the power of available covariates but does not assume data are MAR is proposed. This new hot deck method creates an intuitive sensitivity analysis where imputations may be performed under MAR and under varying MNAR mechanisms, and the resulting impact on inference can be evaluated. In this paper we focus on one particular method for handling missing data: multiple imputation. results.title: Statistical solutions to overcome missing data in clinical trials and observational studies | Editage Insights
results.content: # Statistical solutions to overcome missing data in clinical trials and observational studies. While approaches to handle missing data like last observation carried forward and mean substitution are popular owing to their ease, they are subject to numerous errors, resulting in unreliable data.i,ii It is essential for researchers to be well-versed in appropriate statistical methods that can effectively address missing and incomplete data to ensure the robustness of their study results. This blogpost introduces various statistical methods you can use to mitigate the challenges of missing and incomplete data in observational studies and clinical trials. Multiple imputation is a statistical method that involves creating multiple plausible imputed datasets to account for missing data. (2017) provide a practical guide to when and how multiple imputation can be used for missing data in clinical trials, including flowcharts. Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) is another statistical method that can be used to address missing data. FIML estimates the model parameters by maximizing the likelihood function of the complete data, which includes both observed and missing data. Li and Stuart (2019) discuss the use of both multiple imputation and FIML for missing data in randomized controlled trials. It involves varying the imputation methods or assumptions of the missing data mechanism to evaluate the impact on study results. Pattern mixture models are statistical methods that account for different missing data patterns, such as missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), and missing not at random (MNAR). These models allow for different imputation methods or assumptions of the missing data mechanism depending on the missing data pattern. Pattern mixture models can be used to assess the impact of different missing data mechanisms on study results and provide more robust estimates. Joint modeling is a statistical method that simultaneously models the outcome of interest and the missing data mechanism. Joint modeling can provide more accurate estimates by accounting for the relationship between the outcome and the missing data mechanism, and it can also handle missing data in longitudinal or time-to-event data. (2021) explain the use of joint modeling for handling missing at random data in clinical trials. Do you want to determine the most appropriate method of handling missing data in your study?
